newsitem.title: USA: Brady bill backers hail third anniversary of law.
newsitem.headline: Brady bill backers hail third anniversary of law.

text.p: President Clinton joined supporters of the Brady handgun control law in hailing its third anniversary on Friday, but the National Rifle Association (NRA) said it should be replaced.

The law, named for former White House press secretary James Brady, requires a five-day waiting period for handgun sales for background checks of the buyer unless a state has an instant computer background check system in place.

NRA Executive Vice President Wayne LaPierre said only seven felons had been prosecuted under the Brady law for trying to buy guns in three years even though the attempt is a crime punishable by five years in prison.
"It does absolutely no good to just deny felons, you must arrest them to truly prevent them from getting guns," LaPierre said at a separate news conference.

"Here's a big thumbs up for the Brady law," Brady, speaking from a wheelchair, said at a news conference. He became a gun control advocate after he was shot and crippled during the 1981 attempted assassination of President Ronald Reagan by John Hinckley.
"The law is working exactly as it is intended to work," Brady's wife Sarah, the chair of Handgun Control, added.
Clinton, in a statement, said the bill was one of the most effective public safety measures ever adopted.
"The statistics should end any remaining doubt. The Brady Act is working," he said.
The Justice Department said this week the law had blocked gun sales to 186,000 criminals and others not allowed to buy firearms since it went into effect on this date in 1994.

"It appears the Brady law is making America safer from violent crime," Darrell Sanders, president of the International Association of Chiefs of Police, said, citing reduced rates for crimes committed with guns.
The news conference was held in front of the Supreme Court, which is considering a challenge to the law by several local sheriffs who say they should not be forced to implement a federal law.
LaPierre said most criminals who were blocked from buying weapons at gun stores could get them illegally.

He said the 15 states with instant background systems did a much better job of arresting felons who tried to buy guns and said the other states should replace the five-day waiting period with instant checks.
The five-day waiting period was due to end on Nov. 30, 1998, if a national background check system is ready by then.
Republican leaders promised to try to repeal the Brady law when they took over Congress in 1995, but have been unsuccessful.
